function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that has an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU and runs Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.

> ⚠️ **Prerequisites**
> 
> * You must have a Google Cloud project with billing enabled.
> * The **Compute Engine API** and the **GPU API** must be enabled (`gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com` and `gcloud services enable cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com`).
> * You need a valid **service account key** or you can use the default credentials if you’re running this from a GCP VM or Cloud Shell.
> * The target zone must support GPUs (e.g., `us-central1-b`, `us-east1-c`, `europe-west4-a`, …).  
>   Check the latest list here: https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus#available_zones

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Variables – change these to suit your environment
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-b"
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8"          # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM – adjust as needed
GPU_COUNT=1
GPU_TYPE="nvidia-tesla-a6000"
IMAGE_FAMILY="ubuntu-2004-lts"
IMAGE_PROJECT="ubuntu-os-cloud"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
  --accelerator="type=$GPU_TYPE,count=$GPU_COUNT" \
  --image-family="$IMAGE_FAMILY" \
  --image-project="$IMAGE_PROJECT" \
  --boot-disk-size=100GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
  --tags=http-server,https-server \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM configuration |
| `--accelerator` | Attach GPU(s) |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Base OS image (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS) |
| `--boot-disk-size` | Size of the boot disk |
| `--boot-disk-type` | SSD for better I/O |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script` | Optional script that runs on first boot (e.g., install drivers, CUDA, etc.) |
| `--tags` | Network tags for firewall rules |
| `--scopes` | IAM scopes – gives full cloud‑platform access |

> **Tip:** If you want to use a custom image (e.g., one that already has CUDA installed), replace the `--image-family`/`--image-project` pair with `--image=my-custom-image`.

---

## 2. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine REST API directly (e.g., from a script or a CI/CD pipeline), here’s the exact JSON payload you would POST to:

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-b/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-b/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-b/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update\nsudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-470\n"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
```

### How to POST it

```bash
curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @instance.json \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-b/instances"
```

Replace `@instance.json` with the path to a file containing the JSON above.

---

## 3. After Creation – Verify GPU Availability

Once the instance is running, SSH into it and run:

```bash
ssh ubuntu@<external-ip>
nvidia-smi
```

You should see the RTX A6000 listed with its driver version and GPU utilization.

---

## 4. Optional: Automate GPU Driver Installation

If you want the GPU driver and CUDA toolkit pre‑installed, add a `startup-script` that pulls the NVIDIA driver installer and runs it. Example:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Install NVIDIA driver
wget https://us.download.nvidia.com/XFree86/Linux-x86_64/470.57.02/NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-470.57.02.run
chmod +x NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-470.57.02.run
./NVIDIA-Linux-x86_64-470.57.02.run --silent
# Install CUDA (optional)
wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.7.0-1_amd64.deb
dpkg -i cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.7.0-1_amd64.deb
apt-key adv --fetch-keys https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/7fa2af80.pub
apt-get update
apt-get install -y cuda
```

Save this as `startup.sh` and reference it in the `gcloud` command (`--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh`).

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Project ID & Zone |
| ✅ | Machine type (CPU/RAM) |
| ✅ | GPU type & count |
| ✅ | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| ✅ | Boot disk size/type |
| ✅ | Startup script (optional) |
| ✅ | Firewall tags (HTTP/HTTPS) |
| ✅ | IAM scopes |

That’s all you need to spin up a GPU‑enabled Compute Engine instance with an RTX A6000 and Ubuntu 20.04 LTS. Happy computing!
